newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: White House expects APEC endorsement on infotech.
newsitem.headline: White House expects APEC endorsement on infotech.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton expected Asia-Pacific leaders to strongly endorse his effort to conclude a global agreement on free trade in computers and telecommunications equipment, a U.S. spokesman said on Monday.

Clinton, his prestige and power immensely boosted by his sweeping re-election victory 20 days ago, pitched into a personal lobbying effort with fellow heads of government on Sunday on the eve of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit.

"(Clinton) has been working that issue himself.. when the declaration is read later today, we'll see if they put a little more oomph into this issue than the APEC ministers did," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
The leaders of APEC's 18 member economies were holding a summit on Monday at Subic Bay, a former naval base north of Manila.

An advance copy of a joint declaration to be issued at the end of the summit said leaders called for an agreement on information technology to be concluded at the first meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which regulates world trade, next month.
Such an agreement "should substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000", the declaration said. But it recognised the need for flexibility in the negotiations.
The copy given to reporters in advance did not give any more detail. It was not clear whether the statement was still open to further changes by leaders during their six-hour gathering.

APEC trade and foreign ministers agreed last week to back the U.S. push for an information technology pact by the time of the inaugural WTO meeting in Singapore. But their statement was far from the ringing endorsement Washington had wanted.
The White House spokesman said Clinton personally lobbied his fellow APEC leaders on the issue in a series of face-to-face meetings and at a private dinner on Sunday evening.

"An important goal for the president here at APEC was to seek APEC's active support for a trade liberalisation agreement in the information technology sector that could be successfully concluded by the WTO ministers when they meet next week in Singapore," McCurry said.

Washington originally wanted APEC's endorsement for zero tariffs on information technology trade by the year 2000. The United States says the business is worth at least $500 billion a year, 80 percent of that in the booming Asia-Pacific.
While APEC ministers adopted a watered-down statement on the issue, McCurry indicated that Clinton remained determined to get what he wanted.

"The United States would clearly be delighted if there was a commitment by the WTO ministerial conference that would establish a date certain goal for this substantial elimination of tariffs in the information technology sector," the spokesman said.
